claims.text: Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 normally forms several primary non-eutectic phases.
Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 exhibits a complex multistep crystallization sequence during cooling and reheating.
A trace boron addition will suppress primary crystallization in Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20.
A trace boron addition will promote amorphous-phase retention.
Boron increases chemical disorder in the alloy.
Boron modifies the free-energy landscape and thermodynamic driving forces for crystallization.
The increased disorder raises the nucleation-energy barrier.
A higher nucleation barrier hinders the formation and growth of primary crystalline phases.
Stabilization of the undercooled liquid reduces the propensity for multistep crystallization during reheating.
The boron-doped alloy will have greater amorphous retention than the undoped alloy.
The boron-doped alloy will have improved thermal stability relative to the undoped alloy.
Boron doping will reduce the extent or delay the onset of primary crystallization under rapid cooling.
Boron doping will reduce the extent or delay the onset of primary crystallization under slower cooling followed by reheating.
The base alloy's extensive primary crystallization and multistep transformations limit glass formation and reduce thermal stability.
Rapid cooling above the base alloy's conventional critical threshold can bypass nucleation.
Reheating must remain within temperature boundaries that avoid heterogeneous crystallization for the intervention to be effective.

Failure to produce either a statistically significant increase in amorphous fraction or a delayed or higher crystallization-onset temperature relative to an identically processed undoped control would falsify the hypothesis.
